common_name: Oreja de Burro Vanilla (Papantla, Veracruz Heirloom Vanilla)

planting.note: Plant stem cuttings of at least three nodes in a loose, moist, well-drained bark or orchid medium against a living or constructed support in bright filtered light; Oreja de Burro is a traditional landrace type long selected by Totonac growers around Papantla, Veracruz, Mexico's historic vanilla-growing heartland.

directions: Oreja de Burro, meaning 'donkey's ear,' is a traditional local type of Vanilla planifolia long cultivated by Totonac vanilla growers around Papantla, Veracruz, the region credited with originating cultivated vanilla centuries before it spread to Madagascar and Reunion. Growers distinguish it from other Papantla stock by its notably broad, thick, rounded leaves and plump pods, traits that give rise to its common name. Like all cultivated vanilla it is a hemi-epiphytic climbing orchid that must be trained up a support tree or trellis in warm, humid, partially shaded conditions, and because its natural euglossine bee pollinator does not range outside Mesoamerica, flowers must be hand-pollinated within hours of opening to set pods. Harvest green pods roughly eight to nine months after pollination and cure them using the traditional Totonac method of alternating sun-wilting and sweating in wool blankets over several weeks to develop the pods' dark color and characteristic aroma.
sources: USDA National Plant Germplasm System
Bruman, H.J., 'The Culture History of Mexican Vanilla,' Hispanic American Historical Review

planting.note: Direct sow once soil is thoroughly warm; Tuxpeño is a tall tropical lowland landrace named for Tuxpan, Veracruz, and wants a long, hot, humid growing season with fertile, well-drained soil.

directions: Tuxpeño is one of the most agriculturally important native races of maize in Mexico, originating in the hot, humid Gulf Coast lowlands around Tuxpan, Veracruz, and cataloged among the classic Mexican maize races described by Wellhausen and colleagues in the mid-twentieth century. Plants grow tall and leafy with strong stalks and large ears bearing white or yellow dent kernels, and the race proved so broadly adapted to tropical lowland conditions that it became a foundational parent in international tropical maize breeding, most notably through CIMMYT's long-running Tuxpeño improvement programs. Give it rich, well-drained soil, full sun, and even moisture through tasseling and ear fill, planting in blocks rather than thin rows to ensure good wind pollination. Harvest fresh for milky-stage table use or let ears dry fully on the stalk for grain storage and traditional uses such as tortillas and pozol.
sources: Wellhausen, Roberts, Hernandez & Mangelsdorf, Races of Maize in Mexico (1952)

planting.note: Direct sow after frost danger has passed; Comiteco is a highland landrace named for Comitán, Chiapas, and is traditionally grown at elevation where cool nights slow its long maturation.

directions: Comiteco is a traditional highland race of maize named for the city and district of Comitán in the Chiapas highlands of southern Mexico, where Tzeltal, Tojolabal, and mestizo farmers have long grown it on terraced milpas above roughly 1,500 meters elevation. Compared to lowland Mexican races, Comiteco plants are more medium-statured and the ears carry softer, semi-floury kernels adapted to the cooler, often drier highland growing conditions and longer maturation window of the region. Grow it in fertile, well-worked soil in full sun, watering during dry spells but avoiding waterlogging, and expect a notably long season from planting to full dry-down of the ears. Harvest once husks have browned fully and kernels have hardened, and use the dried grain for tortillas, tamales, and the fermented maize beverage pozol as it traditionally has been.
sources: Wellhausen, Roberts, Hernandez & Mangelsdorf, Races of Maize in Mexico (1952)
CONABIO, Razas de maiz en Mexico

common_name: Jamapa Black Bean (Veracruz-Bred Heirloom Dry Bean)

planting.note: Direct sow once soil has warmed after last frost; Jamapa is a bush-type black bean released from Mexico's Cotaxtla experiment station in Veracruz and grows readily wherever warm-season beans are planted.

directions: Jamapa is a bush black bean released in the early 1970s from Mexico's Campo Experimental Cotaxtla research station near the Jamapa River in Veracruz, for which it is named, and it went on to become one of the most widely planted black bean varieties across Mexico and Central America. It bears small, glossy black seeds on compact, upright plants that set pods reliably even under tropical lowland heat and humidity, traits that also made it an influential parent behind many later Mexican and Central American black bean breeding lines. Grow in full sun on well-drained soil, watering consistently through flowering and pod fill, then withholding water as pods mature and dry. Harvest when most pods have dried and rattle with loose seed, pulling or cutting whole plants to finish drying under cover before threshing for classic frijoles negros, soups, and refried beans.
sources: INIFAP (Instituto Nacional de Investigaciones Forestales, Agricolas y Pecuarias), Campo Experimental Cotaxtla bean breeding records

common_name: Freiherr von Berlepsch Apple (German Heirloom Dessert Apple)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while still dormant in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; provide a compatible pollinizer variety nearby for reliable fruit set.

directions: Freiherr von Berlepsch was raised in Germany around 1880 and named for the German nobleman and pomology patron Hans Hermann Freiherr von Berlepsch, becoming one of the most celebrated dessert apples of the German home orchard tradition. The fruit is medium-sized with yellow-green skin flushed and streaked orange-red, enclosing firm, aromatic, spicy-sweet flesh noted for unusually high vitamin C content among dessert apples. It ripens in mid autumn and keeps well into winter in cool storage, developing a richer, more complex flavor after a few weeks off the tree. The tree can be susceptible to canker and scab in damp climates, so prune for an open canopy with good air circulation, and harvest once fruit detaches easily from the spur with a gentle twist.
sources: Kompetenzzentrum Obstbau-Bodensee (Germany), apple cultivar database
Pomologen-Verein e.V. (German Pomological Society) variety records
Bundesanstalt fur Zuchtungsforschung an Kulturpflanzen, German fruit genebank records

common_name: Goldparmäne Apple (German Heirloom 'King of the Pippins')

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter to early spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; a nearby compatible pollinizer improves fruit set.

directions: Goldparmäne, also known across Europe as King of the Pippins or Reine des Reinettes, is an old dessert apple documented since the eighteenth century and long a fixture of German home orchards under its German name. Fruit is medium and conical, with bright yellow skin heavily flushed orange-red and dotted with fine russeting, enclosing crisp, aromatic flesh with a distinctive nutty sweetness prized for fresh eating. It ripens relatively early, from late summer into early autumn, and is best eaten within a few weeks of harvest since it does not store as long as later-season winter apples. The tree bears reliably once established but can be prone to scab in wet seasons, so site it with good air circulation and full sun, and pick fruit as soon as it separates easily from the spur to catch peak flavor before it turns mealy.
sources: Kompetenzzentrum Obstbau-Bodensee (Germany), apple cultivar database

common_name: Steirischer Ölkürbis (Styrian Oil Pumpkin, Austrian Naked-Seeded Pumpkin)

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant after all frost danger has passed into warm, fertile, well-drained soil with ample room to vine; this Austrian landrace is grown primarily for its hull-less seeds, which are pressed into dark green Kürbiskernöl pumpkin seed oil.

directions: Steirischer Ölkürbis, the Styrian oil pumpkin, is a naked-seeded landrace of Cucurbita pepo developed in Austria's Styria region in the late nineteenth century, where its distinctive flat, dark green, hull-less seeds became the raw material for Kürbiskernöl, the regionally protected pumpkin seed oil of Austrian cuisine. Vines sprawl broadly like other pumpkins and set medium-sized orange-yellow fruit, but growers select and save it chiefly for its seeds rather than its pulp, which is edible but considered secondary to the seed crop. Grow it in warm, fertile soil in full sun with generous room to ramble, and keep it well watered through flowering and fruit set since dry stress reduces seed fill. Harvest once the rind has hardened and the vines begin to die back, then scoop, wash, and dry the seeds thoroughly before roasting or pressing them for oil, or saving them for next year's planting.
sources: European Commission, Protected Geographical Indication 'Steirisches Kürbiskernöl'
Austrian Agricultural Research and Education Centre (AGES) cucurbit variety records
